sources.note: Studies how far a fixed model improves when given more inference compute, and shows that allocating that compute adaptively per prompt by difficulty beats a uniform best-of-N budget by more than 4x.
sources.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters

sources.note: Treats a policy's per-problem failure probability as a random variable over the problem distribution and shows that REINFORCE, pass@K training and MaxRL each optimize a single moment of it, then proposes minimizing the first T moments jointly — which is exactly minimizing the expected truncated number of rollouts needed to reach a first success.
sources.title: Beyond the Mean: Multi-Moment Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning

sources.note: Allocates test-time samples per prompt with a fuzzy controller over human-readable difficulty and confidence signals, and — under a selector-matched protocol that isolates the budget policy from the answer selector — reports the result honestly as an accuracy-compute tradeoff rather than an accuracy gain.
sources.title: Interpretable Adaptive Sampling for LLM Test-Time Scaling

sources.note: Separates how well a policy currently does on a task from how positively that task responds to further training, shows the second is reproducible across independent runs and predicts downstream value at matched current pass rate, and estimates it from a short probe run before RL begins.
sources.title: Beyond Solvability: Task Learnability as a Static Prior for LLM RL Post-Training

sources.note: Feeds a reasoning model's own self-certainty into preference optimization so it compresses confident answers and keeps deliberating on uncertain ones.
sources.title: CAT: Confidence-Adaptive Thinking for Efficient Reasoning of Large Reasoning Models

sources.note: Two-stage fine-tuning that first injects difficulty cues into output prefixes for prospective strategy selection, then injects redundancy cues mid-reasoning for retrospective correction.
sources.title: Think How to Think: Mitigating Overthinking with Autonomous Difficulty Cognition in Large Reasoning Models

sources.note: Fixes reward hacking in hybrid thinking/non-thinking RL by setting per-query token limits for non-thinking responses derived from the solution part of that query's thinking responses.
sources.title: Thinking-Based Non-Thinking: Solving the Reward Hacking Problem in Training Hybrid Reasoning Models via Reinforcement Learning

sources.note: Addresses wasted rollouts in critic-free RL on prompts where every sampled rollout is already correct and the advantage estimate is therefore zero.
sources.title: Miner: Mining Intrinsic Mastery for Data-Efficient RL in Large Reasoning Models

sources.note: Uses elliptical bonuses over a language model's own hidden-state representations as a diversity signal, validates it in a clean inference-time selection setting, then transfers the same signal into RL post-training — where it eliminates the diversity collapse that degrades pass@k at large k.
sources.title: Representation-Based Exploration for Language Models: From Test-Time to Post-Training

sources.note: Stops self-consistency sampling by Bayesian posterior over which answer is the mode, and proves that tracking only the top two answer counts plus an aggregate is enough for asymptotic optimality.
sources.title: Optimal Bayesian Stopping for Efficient Inference of Consistent LLM Answers

sources.note: Trains reasoning models to be concise in proportion to difficulty by modulating the token penalty and the target length per problem, and fixes a distortion that naive reward weighting introduces into group-normalized RL.
sources.title: The Overthinker's DIET: Cutting Token Calories with DIfficulty-AwarE Training

sources.note: Shows that a reasoning model decides how long to think before emitting a single reasoning token — the eventual token count is linearly decodable from the question's activations at Spearman 0.84 — and that this plan is carried by one shared direction vector whose magnitude encodes strength and which acts by shifting the logits of the end-of-thinking token.
sources.title: On Reasoning Strength Planning in Large Reasoning Models

sources.note: Replaces uniform test-time compute allocation with a training-free agent that picks reasoning tools, a search strategy and an exploration parameter per problem, using a process reward model both to prune within a trajectory and to select across iterations.
sources.title: What If We Allocate Test-Time Compute Adaptively?

sources.note: Routes each query to a {model, reasoning budget} configuration by fitting an item response theory model over an evaluation matrix, yielding interpretable query difficulties and configuration abilities, and sending harder queries to higher-ability configurations.
sources.title: RADAR: Reasoning-Ability and Difficulty-Aware Routing for Reasoning LLMs

sources.note: Recasts when-to-stop-reasoning as optimal stopping rather than classification, and proves that a fixed threshold on the probability of being correct can be arbitrarily far from optimal even when that probability is known exactly, because the decision needs the value of continuing and not the value of stopping.
sources.title: OS-Pruner: Pruning Chains-of-Thought of Reasoning Models via Optimal Stopping

instructions:
Write the wiki definition for 'prompt difficulty'.

The sources below are every archived paper and talk that mentions it. Define it as they use it: if they disagree, say so; if the term is used loosely, say that too.

`related` is the one part of the note nothing can work out on its own. The wiki already links entities that turn up in the same summary; what it cannot see is the neighbour a reader would actually want next — the generation before this one, the benchmark it was built to beat, the method it replaces. Name those. Leave the list empty rather than repeating what the sources already put side by side.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

aliases: string - other names the sources use for the same thing
output_schema.definition: string - two to four sentences defining the entity as the cited sources use it, not as a textbook would
output_schema.kind: string - one of: concept, method, dataset, model
related: string - name of a neighbouring entity worth linking to. Kept as you give it and never derived away, so name what a reader should turn to next rather than what happens to appear alongside this. Answering again replaces the whole list; an empty list retracts

result.definition: How hard a problem is for a given policy, and across 15 sources the variable that both training and inference allocation turn on. Its central property is that it is policy-relative and moving: a prompt is easy when every rollout succeeds and hard when none does, and both cases produce zero group-relative advantage, so the useful band is the middle -- one method shifts 82.7 percent of its gradient budget into the 0.2-0.9 pass-rate band against a baseline's 58.9. It also moves during training, which is why one source tracks per-task reward trajectories across 20 epochs and classifies tasks into six profiles including forgetting and stubbornly-unlearned rather than treating difficulty as a static label. At inference the same variable governs allocation, with several methods conditioning the thinking budget on it, and one finding the saving concentrated on the easy tail -- 53 to 81 percent token reduction for the top decile and percentile. Two cautions the archive attaches. Difficulty defined by a baseline's own pass rate selects for that baseline's failures, so part of any tiered improvement is regression toward the mean. And benchmark difficulty is only an approximation of what a particular policy can answer, which is why the better sources report tiers by measured pass rate rather than by benchmark label.
